title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

hypotheses.text: A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type.
hypotheses.label: A1. Trust in the sharer → sharing

hypotheses.text: A1. The slope of plausibility on trust in the sharer, by information type.
hypotheses.label: A1. Trust in the sharer → plausibility

hypotheses.text: A1. The close-tie premium on sharing, net of the other source attributes, by information type.
hypotheses.label: A1. Close tie → sharing

hypotheses.text: A2. Sharing without believing: among profiles chosen to share, the probability that the respondent judged the other post more plausible, by information type, net of source attributes, media trust and age.
hypotheses.label: A2. Sharing without believing

hypotheses.text: A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls.
hypotheses.label: A3. Co-ideological sharer → sharing

hypotheses.text: A4. Ego-network composition: the respondent's six named contacts as a measured network. Among misinformation profiles, sharing on the network's mean perceived belief in disputed claims, net of network ideological spread, mean trust, age and ideology. Each misinformation profile is weighted by 1 / the respondent's number of them, which reproduces the respondent-level regression of the misinformation-sharing rate.
hypotheses.label: A4. Ego-network conspiracy load → sharing misinformation

hypotheses.text: B1. Message x respondent congruence: among partisan respondents shown partisan-slanted headlines, sharing of congenial against uncongenial content (headline slant from the paper's preliminary automated coding), by information type.
hypotheses.label: B1. Congenial content → sharing

hypotheses.text: B2. A conspiracy-prone source: the slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims (0-1), net of the other source attributes, by information type.
hypotheses.label: B2. Conspiracy-prone sharer → sharing

hypotheses.text: B2. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims, by information type.
hypotheses.label: B2. Conspiracy-prone sharer → plausibility

hypotheses.text: B2, claim-specific (thin): for the anti-vaccine (polio) misinformation headline, plausibility when the sharer is seen as believing 'Covid-19 vaccines modify your DNA' against not.
hypotheses.label: B2. Sharer believes the vaccine claim → plausibility of anti-vaccine misinformation

hypotheses.text: B3. Health vs. political misinformation: among misinformation profiles, the trust slope on sharing for health (guanabana, polio) and political headlines.
hypotheses.label: B3. Trust → sharing misinformation, health vs. political

hypotheses.text: B3. Among misinformation profiles, the close-tie premium for health and political headlines.
hypotheses.label: B3. Close tie → sharing misinformation, health vs. political

hypotheses.text: B4. Sharer origin (continental US vs. elsewhere) and sharing, by survey language and by the respondent's nativity.
hypotheses.label: B4. Sharer origin → sharing, by language and nativity

ambiguities.pap_text: Regress DV on information type (placebo, misinformation, fact-check), closeness of tie, national origin/nativity, perceived trust, perceived political knowledge, ideology, and beliefs in disputed claims
ambiguities.interpretation: One additive OLS with all seven features as categorical factors; each feature is reported as its own hypothesis (treatment = that feature, covariates = the other six), which reproduces the joint model's AMCEs. Feature levels follow the authors' coding: trust and knowledge binned low (1-2), mid (3), high (4-5); belief in disputed claims split at the median; 'Don't know' sharer ideology coded moderate.
alternatives: trust, knowledge and disputed beliefs as linear terms
ambiguities.reason: The plan does not say how the measured attributes are coded.

ambiguities.pap_text: re-weighting the AMCE to account for different assignment probabilities associated with the meta-data fields
ambiguities.interpretation: For each source attribute, a stabilized inverse of its realized marginal assignment probability among complete cases (weights normalized to mean 1); the attribute's AMCE is re-estimated from the full weighted model. A joint six-way re-weighting is degenerate in these data.
ambiguities.reason: The plan names the goal, not the weights.

ambiguities.pap_text: subset analyses using age, ideology, beliefs in disputed claims, trust in media, and survey language (marginal means). Tertile splits comparing upper and lower tertiles
ambiguities.interpretation: For each moderator, the difference in marginal means (Pr chosen) of every feature level between the highest and lowest tertile (Spanish minus English for survey language), from a cell-means model with respondent-clustered SEs. Tertiles are formed over shown profiles; ideology is the respondent's 5-point self-placement.
ambiguities.reason: The plan names the estimand (marginal means) but not the test.

ambiguities.interpretation: Unweighted; the YouGov survey weight is not used.
ambiguities.reason: The plan does not mention survey weights.
